passage:
The history of jazz piano has long been narrated as a sequence of heroic solo innovators — Jelly Roll Morton, Earl Hines, Art Tatum — each superseding the last in technical virtuosity. Standard accounts treat the instrument's role in jazz as essentially soloistic: the piano stands apart from the rhythm section when it steps forward, and the pianist's task is to dazzle. The truth is that this received narrative, however seductive, obscures what may be the more consequential development in the tradition: the gradual transformation of jazz piano from a vehicle for individual display into a medium of collective conversation.

That transformation is most audible in the work of the bebop pianists of the 1940s. Thelonious Monk and Bud Powell are often cited as the period's towering figures, and for good reason — their harmonic innovations alone would secure their legacies. But the standard account tends to frame those innovations in soloist's terms: Monk's dissonant, angular voicings are praised as idiosyncratic personal signatures, and Powell's fleet single-note lines are measured against the virtuoso pianists who preceded him. What such framings miss is the degree to which both pianists were reconceiving the piano's relationship to the ensemble. Monk, notoriously, would stop comping entirely when a horn soloist took a chorus, allowing silence to function as a form of harmonic suggestion. Powell, meanwhile, developed a left-hand sparseness that opened the piano's interior register to the bass and drums, effectively inviting the rhythm section into a space the stride pianists had monopolized. These were not merely technical refinements; they were gestures of relinquishment, a willingness to let the collective voice supersede the individual one.

This shift carries implications that reach beyond bebop. The modal jazz of Miles Davis's late 1950s recordings relocated harmonic responsibility away from the piano entirely, distributing it across the ensemble; and the free jazz of the 1960s pushed further still, dissolving the very hierarchy that had placed the piano at the center of jazz harmony. Yet each of these subsequent developments was prefigured — and made imaginable — by the bebop pianists' earlier willingness to create productive vacancies in the musical texture. The solo tradition, in other words, generated the conditions of its own partial eclipse.

To read jazz piano history as a story of escalating individual achievement, then, is to mistake the surface of the music for its deeper logic. The pianists who matter most to the tradition's evolution were those who understood that to cede ground — harmonically, rhythmically, spatially within the ensemble — was not a retreat from artistry but its highest expression: a faith in the conversation that only restraint makes possible.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Thelonious Monk and Bud Powell were more technically accomplished pianists than the stride pianists who preceded them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The received narrative of jazz piano as a succession of virtuoso soloists misrepresents the tradition's deeper development toward collective musical conversation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Modal jazz and free jazz represent the most significant departures from the soloist tradition in jazz piano history.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jazz piano underwent a series of technical refinements in the 1940s that improved the instrument's integration with the rhythm section.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The history of jazz should be understood primarily in terms of how ensembles, rather than individual musicians, shaped the music's evolution.

explanations.correct: The passage opens by identifying the 'received narrative' of heroic soloists as misleading, then argues across four paragraphs that the tradition's deeper logic is one of collective conversation enabled by deliberate restraint. B integrates both the critique of the standard account and the positive claim.
explanations.A: Too narrow — the comparison to stride pianists is a supporting detail, not the main point.
explanations.C: Modal and free jazz are mentioned as later developments prefigured by bebop, not as the passage's central thesis.
explanations.D: 'Technical refinements' is a phrase the passage explicitly rejects as a sufficient description of what bebop pianists did.
explanations.E: The passage focuses on jazz piano specifically, not jazz history writ large, and frames the argument around individual pianists' choices rather than ensembles as such.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the standard account of jazz piano history can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: unqualified rejection of its characterization of bebop pianists

choices.label: B
choices.text: appreciative of its identification of key figures while skeptical of its interpretive framework

choices.label: C
choices.text: indifferent to its claims about virtuosity but accepting of its chronological ordering

choices.label: D
choices.text: admiration for the richness of its historical detail

choices.label: E
choices.text: hostility toward the scholars who have promoted it

explanations.correct: The author concedes that Monk and Powell are 'cited as the period's towering figures, and for good reason' before arguing that the standard account 'misses' their collective contributions. This is classic qualified acceptance of names/facts with skepticism toward interpretation. B captures both moves.
explanations.A: Too strong — the author does not reject the standard account wholesale; it grants the pianists' importance.
explanations.C: The author is far from indifferent; skepticism toward the interpretive framework is a sustained concern.
explanations.D: The passage never praises the standard account's historical detail; it questions its interpretive logic.
explanations.E: No hostility toward scholars is expressed; the critique is aimed at the narrative framework, not its proponents.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A historical claim is introduced, challenged by a series of counterexamples, and ultimately conceded to be partly correct.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A received interpretive framework is identified, a richer alternative is developed through specific cases, later historical evidence is marshaled in support, and a broader conclusion is drawn.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing theories about jazz piano are presented in equal depth, and the passage ends without adjudicating between them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A biography of Thelonious Monk and Bud Powell is given, followed by a discussion of their influence on later jazz.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A narrow claim about bebop piano technique is stated and then generalized to all forms of twentieth-century American music.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 identifies the received soloist narrative; paragraph 2 develops the alternative (collective conversation) through Monk and Powell; paragraph 3 marshals modal and free jazz as corroborating subsequent developments; paragraph 4 draws the broader conclusion about restraint as artistry. B tracks this four-paragraph sequence accurately.
explanations.A: The passage never concedes that the received account is 'partly correct' in its interpretive logic; it only concedes the importance of individual figures.
explanations.C: The passage clearly adjudicates — it argues that the collective-conversation reading is superior.
explanations.D: The passage discusses Monk and Powell analytically, not biographically, and does not end with 'influence' as the main concern.
explanations.E: The claim is about jazz piano specifically, not all twentieth-century American music.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Monk's practice of stopping comping when a horn soloist took a chorus was significant because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: demonstrated a technical inability to accompany horn players effectively

choices.label: B
choices.text: allowed silence to operate as a mode of harmonic suggestion within the ensemble

choices.label: C
choices.text: reflected the influence of the stride piano tradition he was seeking to revive

choices.label: D
choices.text: was adopted directly from the modal jazz approach Miles Davis later popularized

choices.label: E
choices.text: shifted the harmonic burden entirely to the bass and drums

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that Monk 'would stop comping entirely when a horn soloist took a chorus, allowing silence to function as a form of harmonic suggestion.' B is a close paraphrase.
explanations.A: The passage nowhere suggests Monk lacked technical ability; the gesture is interpreted as a deliberate artistic choice.
explanations.C: Stride pianists are the tradition being departed from, not revived.
explanations.D: The causal direction is reversed — bebop pianists prefigured modal jazz, not the other way around.
explanations.E: The passage says Powell's left-hand sparseness opened space for bass and drums; Monk's silence is described as harmonic suggestion, not a transfer of harmonic burden.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements about artistic restraint in jazz piano?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Restraint is valuable in jazz piano only when it is accompanied by exceptional technical virtuosity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The willingness to cede harmonic and rhythmic space within an ensemble can itself constitute a form of artistic mastery.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pianists who practiced restraint were generally less respected by their contemporaries than those who favored individual display.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restraint in jazz piano was primarily a response to commercial pressures rather than an aesthetic choice.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tradition of collective musical conversation ultimately proved less influential than the soloist tradition it partially displaced.

explanations.correct: The passage's final paragraph directly states that ceding ground 'was not a retreat from artistry but its highest expression.' B is a precise inference from this claim.
explanations.A: The passage does not condition restraint's value on virtuosity; the two are treated as separable concerns.
explanations.C: The passage says nothing about how contemporaries regarded these pianists; this introduces an evaluative frame absent from the text.
explanations.D: Commercial pressures are never mentioned; the passage frames restraint as purely an aesthetic-ethical choice.
explanations.E: The passage argues the opposite — that the solo tradition generated the conditions for a collective one, implying significant influence of the latter.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to Powell's left-hand sparseness (second paragraph) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate how a bebop pianist's individual innovation helped open ensemble space for other instruments

choices.label: B
choices.text: argue that Powell was technically inferior to stride pianists who preceded him

choices.label: C
choices.text: contrast Powell's approach with Monk's in order to show that they pursued incompatible goals

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that bebop piano was primarily a reaction against the limitations of the rhythm section

choices.label: E
choices.text: support the claim that bebop pianists were more interested in the bass than in harmonic innovation

explanations.correct: The passage introduces Powell's left-hand sparseness as evidence that bebop pianists were reconceiving the piano's relationship to the ensemble — specifically that it 'invited the rhythm section into a space the stride pianists had monopolized.' A captures this rhetorical function: the detail illustrates the broader claim about collective musical conversation.
explanations.B: The passage never implies inferiority; the sparseness is framed as an advance in collective thinking.
explanations.C: The passage treats Monk and Powell as parallel examples of the same impulse, not as opposing figures.
explanations.D: The passage does not frame bebop as a reaction against the rhythm section's limitations; if anything, bebop opened space for the rhythm section.
explanations.E: No claim about the bass being more important than harmonic innovation is made or implied.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's central claim about the significance of bebop pianists to jazz history?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several modal jazz composers have stated in interviews that the harmonic models they inherited came primarily from bebop horn players, not pianists.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recordings from the late 1950s and 1960s document that bassists and drummers played more melodically active parts when performing alongside bebop pianists who practiced restraint than when accompanying more harmonically dense pianists.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bud Powell's early recordings show that he began his career imitating stride pianists before developing his signature left-hand sparseness.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Free jazz musicians of the 1960s have consistently denied any meaningful connection to bebop as a stylistic precursor.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thelonious Monk composed many of his most celebrated pieces as solo piano works intended for performance without an ensemble.

explanations.correct: The author's central claim is that bebop pianists' restraint enabled collective musical conversation within the ensemble. B directly supports this by providing evidence that other instrumentalists' roles expanded in response to that restraint — confirming the causal and collective mechanism the author argues for.
explanations.A: This would weaken the author's claim by suggesting bebop pianists were not the primary channel through which collective harmonic thinking reached later jazz.
explanations.C: This is a biographical detail about Powell's development that neither strengthens nor weakens the claim about restraint's significance; it is neutral at best.
explanations.D: This would weaken the author's argument in paragraph 3 that bebop prefigured free jazz.
explanations.E: This would actually complicate the author's framing of Monk as an ensemble-oriented thinker, potentially weakening the claim.
